title: Cosmic Fireworks in Ultraviolet
caption: The Eta Carinae star system in ultraviolet light, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, N. Smith (University of Arizona, Tucson), and J. Morse (BoldlyGo Institute, New York)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Two dusty bubbles bulge out in opposite directions, wrapped in blue glowing gas and edged with red filaments. This is the nebula around Eta Carinae, a star system prone to violent outbursts. The bubbles were formed by material ejected during one such episode in the 1840s.

This view uses ultraviolet light, captured by Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. It revealed the glow of magnesium in warm gas, shown in blue, in places astronomers had not seen it before. The magnesium lies between the dusty bubbles and the outer filaments, which are rich in nitrogen and heated by shocks, shown in red.

The blue region outside the lower-left bubble is crossed by streaks. They form where the star's light pokes through clumps of dust on the bubble's surface. Where ultraviolet light hits the dense dust, it casts a long, thin shadow out into the surrounding gas.
scale: Eta Carinae lies 7500 light-years away, according to the caption.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in ultraviolet and visible light. Magnesium glow in warm gas is shown in blue and nitrogen-rich filaments in red.
understand.eye: Much of this light is ultraviolet, which the eye cannot see and which Earth's atmosphere blocks.

explore: Telescopes including Hubble have monitored the Eta Carinae system for more than two decades. The outburst that produced the two bubbles took place in the 1840s.
alt: Two dusty bipolar bubbles surrounded by blue glowing gas with streaks and outer red filaments.
